The answer to "when did women get the vote" depends on the country and context. In the United States, women's suffrage was established nationally with the ratification of the 19th Amendment on August 18, 1920, certified on August 26, 1920 [d1][d5][d8]. However, full enfranchisement was not immediate for all women: Native American women gained citizenship rights in 1924, and the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was needed to overcome barriers preventing racial minorities from exercising their voting rights [d5]. Earlier still, some U.S. states had granted women voting rights before 1920 — New Jersey's 1776 constitution enfranchised property-owning women, and 22 states had extended voting rights to women prior to the 19th Amendment [d3][d6][d8]. Globally, the timeline varied widely: British women over 30 gained the vote in 1918, French women in 1944, and Bhutan held its first national elections including women only in 2008, while at least 20 nations preceded the U.S. in granting women the right to vote nationally [d2][d10].
